question: What causes Dutch roll?

options.text: Too much longitudinal stability in pitch at high speed
A rearward CG beyond the aft limit
Turbulence acting on the elevators only
The interplay of lateral (roll) and directional (yaw) stability

explanation: Dutch roll comes from the coupling between stability in roll and stability in yaw: a disturbance in one axis causes a secondary disturbance in the other.

question: Which relationship between stabilities makes Dutch roll likely?

options.text: Lateral stability greater than directional stability
Directional stability greater than lateral stability
Equal lateral and longitudinal stability
Longitudinal stability greater than lateral stability

explanation: If lateral (roll) stability exceeds directional (yaw) stability, the aircraft is prone to Dutch roll. The opposite imbalance leads towards spiral instability.

question: An aircraft yaws after a gust. Why does it then roll?

options.text: The retreating wing goes faster and gains lift
The advancing wing goes faster and gains lift
The fin produces a rolling moment directly
The ailerons move with the yaw

explanation: The wing moving forward travels faster through the air and makes more lift, the other wing less, so the aircraft rolls.

question: In Dutch roll, what produces the yawing moment that reverses the motion?

options.text: Parasite drag on the fin
Less induced drag on the raised, faster-moving wing
More induced drag on the raised, faster wing
The rudder moving with the roll

explanation: The higher-lift wing also has more induced drag, which yaws the aircraft back against the original disturbance, and the cycle repeats the other way.

question: Why does wing sweep make Dutch roll worse?

options.text: The advancing wing's effective sweep rises, cutting its lift
The advancing wing's effective sweep falls, raising its lift
Sweep reduces the fin's area
Sweep moves the CG aft

explanation: In a yaw the forward-going wing has less effective sweep and makes more lift, while the retreating wing has more effective sweep and less lift, strengthening the roll.

question: Why is the aerodynamic damping of Dutch roll weaker at high altitude?

options.text: The air is warmer at high altitude
The available rudder travel is reduced at high altitude
Higher TAS means a smaller angle of attack change for a given disturbance
The fin is less effective at low TAS

explanation: At altitude TAS is higher for the same IAS, so a given yaw rate changes the fin's angle of attack less, and the corrective force, and the damping, are smaller.

question: Instead of enlarging the stabilising surfaces, how is Dutch roll at altitude usually controlled?

options.text: The spoilers are deployed in cruise
The ailerons are rigged with more up travel
The aircraft is flown with its CG further aft in cruise
A yaw damper applies small, rapid rudder corrections

explanation: Larger fins would add drag. A yaw damper senses the yaw and applies rapid, small and effective rudder deflections that stop the Dutch roll before it builds.

question: How is the yaw damper related to the autopilot?

options.text: It is the autopilot's third axis, or added to it
It is the autopilot's pitch channel
It is unrelated to the autopilot
It replaces the autopilot's roll channel entirely

explanation: The yaw damper is either the third axis of the autopilot or an addition to the third axis of autopilot control.

question: When is the yaw damper normally used?

options.text: For the whole flight
Only during the approach
Only with the autopilot engaged
Only above FL250

explanation: The yaw damper is on for the whole flight. It also helps turn coordination, runway alignment and asymmetric thrust.

question: Why do many large airliners have two or three yaw dampers?

options.text: The autopilot needs one per channel
Without one they must fly much lower to control Dutch roll
One is needed for each engine
Each pilot needs a separate yaw damper of their own

explanation: Many large airliners have poor Dutch roll characteristics. With the yaw damper failed, the only way to control it is to fly much lower, where TAS is reduced.

question: What senses yaw for the yaw damper?

options.text: The flux valve
The air data computer's sideslip vane
A single-axis rate gyro, or the IRS
A pendulous accelerometer on the fin

explanation: A single-axis rate gyro, or in modern aircraft an IRS input, senses the motion about the normal axis so that a correction can be applied quickly.

question: Why is phase advance used in a yaw damper?

options.text: To add rudder in the same sense as the yaw, to speed it up
To delay the rudder until the yaw stops
To make the rudder move more slowly
To apply rudder when the yaw rate is greatest

explanation: Damping must be applied at the maximum rate of disturbance. Phase advance speeds up the signal so the rudder acts at maximum yaw and the input is removed quickly to avoid overcorrecting.

question: What happens if yaw damper rudder is applied just as the fin starts to return the aircraft?

options.text: The yaw is damped perfectly, with no overshoot
The autopilot disconnects
The two forces combine and overcorrect
The rudder has no effect

explanation: Applied at that moment, rudder and fin act together, overcorrecting and making the aircraft overshoot, which is why the signal is phase advanced.

question: Without a filter, how would a yaw damper react to a normal turn?

options.text: It would oppose the turn, making it uncoordinated
It would disconnect itself
It would add exactly the right amount of rudder for the turn
It would not respond at all

explanation: A turn includes yaw, so the yaw damper would see it as a disturbance and apply opposite rudder, making the turn uncoordinated.

question: Which yaw motion should the yaw damper act on?

options.text: Steady rates of turn only
Motion at the Dutch roll frequency only
High-frequency vibration of the airframe
All yaw motion of any frequency

explanation: The yaw damper must let the Dutch roll frequency through to the rudder and block other frequencies, so it does not resist commanded turns.

question: How would you describe the Dutch roll frequency?

options.text: Very high, the same for all aircraft
Zero in a steady turn only
Equal to the engine rotation frequency, which is very high
Relatively low, slightly different for each type

explanation: The Dutch roll frequency is based on the aircraft's natural yawing frequency. It is relatively low and differs slightly between types.

question: In a steady, constant-rate turn, what is the Dutch roll filter's output?

options.text: A rising signal for as long as the turn lasts
Zero, so there is no rudder demand
A steady signal aiding the turn
A steady signal opposing the turn

explanation: The output builds while the rate of turn builds, then falls to zero once the rate is constant, so a steady turn gives no rudder demand. On rolling out the opposite pulse appears.

question: With a split rudder, one of two yaw dampers fails. What protection remains?

options.text: None; both rudder halves stop
Full protection, from the other damper
Double, because the other doubles its gain
About half the original yaw damping

explanation: Each yaw damper drives one part of the rudder, so with one failed only half the yaw damper protection remains. This is allowed for in design and operation.

question: Why may the yaw damper gain be scheduled by the air data computer?

options.text: To give more authority at high speed
To allow for the aircraft's weight
To avoid overstressing at high speed
To correct for the CG position

explanation: Even a small rudder input can overstress the aircraft in some conditions, so CADC data scales the gain, reducing yaw damper authority at high speed.

question: What is the purpose of synchronisation before yaw damper engagement?

options.text: To prevent engagement transients
To test the hydraulic supply
To align the rate gyro with north
To centre the rudder pedals

explanation: An inverting integrator cancels any servomotor output before engagement, so no transient kicks the rudder when the yaw damper engages.

question: In the engaged yaw damper, what does the bandpass filter do?

options.text: Passes the Dutch roll frequency and blocks others
Converts the signal to DC
Blocks the Dutch roll frequency
Passes all frequencies from the gyro to the rudder

explanation: The bandpass filter passes only the yaw damper frequency, so the yaw damper does not oppose turns and does not respond to vibration or bending.

question: What is the typical maximum rudder deflection of a yaw damper?

options.text: 25° either way
3–4° either way
Full rudder travel
10–15° either way

explanation: The yaw damper's rudder authority is small, typically 3–4° in either direction, enough to damp Dutch roll without hazard.

question: What is the LVDT used for in a yaw damper?

options.text: Testing the hydraulic pressure
Sensing the rate of yaw
Rudder position feedback
Measuring sideslip angle

explanation: The linear variable differential transformer feeds back rudder position, cancelling the processed gyro signal when the rudder has moved enough for the yaw rate.

question: In a strong crosswind, how does the yaw damper still return the rudder to neutral?

options.text: The yaw damper disconnects itself in strong crosswinds
The pilot centres the rudder by hand
The rate gyro is caged
An integrator ramps up the position feedback

explanation: If position feedback is too small to recentre the rudder against the crosswind, an integrator ramps up the feedback until the rudder returns to neutral, then runs down.

question: How does the yaw damper test switch work?

options.text: It cuts off the hydraulic power to the rudder actuator
It moves the rudder pedals directly
It torques the rate gyro to simulate a yaw
It sends a signal to the flux valve

explanation: Selecting the test switch applies a voltage to the rate gyro's torquing coil, simulating aircraft yaw; the rudder position indicator then responds.

question: The yaw damper test switch is moved left and held, then released. What does the indicator show?

options.text: Left then centre; on release, right then centre
Right then centre; on release, left then centre
No movement until release
Left and stays left until release

explanation: Holding left, the indicator moves left and back to centre; on release it moves right and back to centre. The reverse happens for a right test.

question: Which faults can light a yaw damper failure light?

options.text: Engine failure on one side
Rudder pedal movement made by the pilot in flight
Autopilot disengagement
Loss of hydraulic or electrical power, or the gyro input

explanation: The light covers loss of hydraulic or electrical power, logic failures and loss of the rate gyro input. The switch then isolates that yaw damper.

question: Why is a failed yaw damper switched off?

options.text: To restore full rudder authority to it
To avoid spurious rudder inputs
To transfer control to the autopilot
To reset its rate gyro

explanation: Isolating an inoperative yaw damper stops it making spurious rudder inputs.

question: What does the small rudder trim indicator for each yaw damper show?

options.text: The sideslip angle
The yaw damper's demands on the rudder
The rate of turn
The rudder trim set by the pilot on the trim panel

explanation: It moves left and right of centre to show the yaw damper's rudder demands. It is mainly used when testing the yaw dampers before flight.

question: How can a yaw damper without a test switch be checked?

options.text: It cannot be checked at all before flight
By the maintenance crew only
Only in flight at cruise altitude
By its response to yaw during taxi turns

explanation: Some aircraft rely on taxi turns: in a left turn the yaw damper signal moves left, the rudder moves left and the signal returns to neutral.
